title: IBM Cuts Revenue Forecast as AI Spending Shift Hammers Mainframe Business
excerpt: The tech giant lowered its 2026 growth outlook to 4%-5% after mainframe sales plunged 42% and enterprise clients redirected budgets toward AI infrastructure, confirming a profit warning that triggered the worst stock drop in IBM's history.
body:
• IBM cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast to 4%-5%, down from more than 5%, after a second quarter marred by a 42% plunge in mainframe sales.
  • The company posted Q2 revenue of $17.16 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.93, missing Wall Street estimates on both measures.
  • CEO Arvind Krishna said clients redirected budgets toward AI infrastructure, calling the missed deals "deferred, not destroyed," with a third already closing in Q3.
  • IBM maintained its free cash flow guidance, expecting an increase of about $1 billion year over year, offering a rare bright spot in an otherwise downbeat report.

IBM Trims Full-Year Outlook After Brutal Quarter

IBM on Wednesday formally cut its full-year revenue growth forecast to a range of 4% to 5%, down from prior guidance of more than 5%, after a second quarter in which enterprise clients abruptly shifted spending toward AI-focused data-center hardware at the expense of the company's software and mainframe businesses.

https://x.com/globeandmail/status/2080027448566223006

The Armonk, New York-based technology giant reported second-quarter revenue of $17.16 billion, up just 1% year over year and well below the $17.58 billion analysts had expected, according to LSEG data. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.93 per share, missing the consensus estimate of $2.97. Net profit for the quarter was $2.17 billion, a dip from a year earlier.

The results confirmed what IBM had previewed in a rare mid-quarter profit warning last week — a disclosure that triggered a 25% single-day stock collapse, the worst in the 115-year-old company's history, and erased roughly $67 billion in market value.

Mainframe Business Bears the Brunt

The sharpest pain came from IBM's infrastructure segment, where revenue fell 7% to $3.84 billion. Sales of Z mainframes — the backbone of transaction processing at banks, airlines, and government agencies — cratered 42%.

"That mainframe stack of hardware and transaction processing software impacted IBM's growth by over five points in the quarter. We were only expecting about a point or two of an impact."

— James Kavanaugh, IBM Chief Financial Officer, to Reuters

Software revenue rose 5% to $7.76 billion but still missed the $7.88 billion average estimate. Consulting revenue was flat. The company said clients had "redirected spending towards servers, storage, and memory purchases to secure supply-constrained infrastructure ahead of expected price increases," according to CFO Kavanaugh on the earnings call, as reported by MarketWatch.

AI Spending: A Double-Edged Sword

The quarterly miss highlights a growing tension in enterprise technology: the scramble for AI hardware is squeezing budgets for traditional software and services. IBM's CEO Arvind Krishna told investors on Wednesday's earnings call that the company is "in the early innings of a structural shift for business," according to Barron's.

Krishna said "tens of large deals" failed to close on expected timelines, with the majority involving large capital expenditure agreements at major clients. He framed the setback as temporary rather than existential.

"A lot of the demand is deferred, not destroyed."

— Arvind Krishna, IBM CEO

About one-third of those slipped deals have already closed in the current third quarter, Krishna added. IBM also pointed to its AI consulting pipeline as a positive signal, noting that artificial intelligence represented more than half of all consulting signings in Q2.

Free Cash Flow Holds, Stock Steadies

In a quarter with few bright spots, IBM maintained its full-year free cash flow guidance, reaffirming expectations for an increase of about $1 billion year over year. The company spent $1.6 billion on its dividend in Q2 alone.

Shares initially rose more than 2% in after-hours trading before dipping about 1%. The stock had closed the regular session down 2.3% at $205.77 — its lowest close since November 2024. IBM shares are now down roughly 30% year to date.

Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani called the updated guidance "better than feared," noting he had expected the company to revise growth down to the low-to-mid single digits. CFRA analyst Brooks Idlet said IBM's software struggles likely reflect "specific IBM-related hardware issues" rather than a broader sector weakness.

The Mainframe Moat Under Pressure

The longer-term question for IBM centers on whether the AI revolution will erode the company's historically durable mainframe franchise. IBM stock had already slid in February after AI startup Anthropic released a COBOL modernization playbook for its Claude Code tool, raising the prospect that AI could simplify migration away from the decades-old systems that have long anchored IBM's recurring revenue.

Krishna pushed back on that narrative, telling analysts the company sees "no evidence of clients moving off a mainframe" and expects "significant outperformance in the program to continue through the second half."

What Comes Next

For IBM's large Indian-origin workforce — spanning operations in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune, as well as tens of thousands of Indian-origin professionals in the United States — the company's pivot toward AI execution carries direct implications. Consulting and software, the two segments IBM is counting on for growth, employ a significant share of the company's India-based and diaspora talent.

Krishna, who was born in Andhra Pradesh and holds degrees from IIT Kanpur and the University of Illinois, now faces a credibility test with Wall Street. Investors are watching whether slipped deals convert to real revenue in Q3 and whether IBM can prove the AI pivot complements rather than cannibalizes its existing business. The company's next quarterly update in October will be critical.
